newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Take a pay cut, Brazil's Cardoso urges lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Take a pay cut, Brazil's Cardoso urges lawmakers.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in an interview published on Tuesday said lawmakers should follow his example and accept a pay cut as part of a civil service reform bill stuck in Congress.

Cardoso criticised "reactionary" lawmakers who defeated a key element of the reform last week and said they were defending "absurd" perks of civil servants. "They kick up a fuss in Congress, thinking they're defending the interest of the workers, but in fact they're hurting Brazil," he said in comments to a regional radio station reported in newspapers.

He said he was prepared to sacrifice some of the $5,000 monthly pension he receives as a former university lecturer to comply with a proposed $10,200 a month ceiling on combined pay and pensions proposed in the civil service reform bill.
"The time has come for every one of us to lose a little. Of course no one likes that," added Cardoso, who earns about $8,000 a month in pay as president.

An estimated 140 members of the lower house of Congress earn handsome pensions from previous public sector posts on top of their salaries. Resentment over the ceiling was widely seen as the main factor behind a major administration defeat last week when the lower house failed to muster enough votes to kill an opposition amendment to the civil service reform.

The bill aims to reduce public sector payroll spending, which in some states eats up all receipts. But the amendment struck down a key article that would have let federal and local governments hire new workers without offering them the jobs-for-life guarantees enjoyed by existing civil servants.
Sensing a rebellion in its volatile, multi-party alliance, the government called off further voting on amendments.

"These reforms are for the people because they give a better (fiscal) outlook, interest rates can fall and the Real (currency) becomes more stable and gives more food to the people," Cardoso said in the interview.

In his two years in office, Cardoso has cut Brazil's once rampant inflation to below 10 percent a year. He enjoys strong popularity but has so far failed to get Congress to approve reforms to streamline the state bureaucracy, which are viewed as crucial to the long-term success of his economic plan.
